site.name: RetroClips
site.tagline: Ten seconds of film history. Twenty seconds of why it matters.
site.generated_note: Commentary below is written in the auto-generation pipeline's target style (see scripts/generate_commentary.py). It is example output for this prototype, not live model output.
site.narration_voice_note: ElevenLabs voice used by scripts/generate_narration.py. To switch narrators: change this ID, then re-run the script (no code edit needed).

films.title: Nosferatu
films.scene_description: Count Orlok looms into Ellen's room at the window, rising into the clawed-hand silhouette that became the film's signature image.
films.commentary: This single pose — Schreck's silhouette, fingers splayed into claws against the window light — is the most reproduced image from the entire film, used on posters and in textbooks ever since. Murnau builds to it with almost a minute of unbroken tension, then holds the shape just long enough to burn it into memory.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1922, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
films.scene_description: Caligari hypnotically calls the somnambulist Cesare out of his trance in one sustained close-up, just before unveiling him to the fairground crowd.
films.commentary: Conrad Veidt holds this single unbroken close-up for the better part of a minute, letting the kohl-rimmed eyes and painted-on shadows do all the acting — no cuts, no reaction shots, just Caligari's voice calling him out of the dark. It's one of the earliest horror films to trust stillness over movement to unsettle an audience.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The General
films.scene_description: A full-size steam locomotive plunges through a burning bridge in a single unfaked take.
films.commentary: That's not a miniature — Keaton actually dropped a full locomotive through a burning bridge, once, on camera, with no retakes possible. It was the single most expensive shot of the entire silent era. No stunt double, no trick photography, just a director who insisted the danger had to be real.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: His Girl Friday
films.scene_description: Hildy and Walter trade rapid, overlapping dialogue in his editor's office as he works to talk her out of quitting.
films.commentary: Hawks clocked this dialogue at nearly 240 words a minute, with actors deliberately talking over each other's lines. Most screenplays don't survive that; his did, because the overlaps were scripted, not improvised. It's still the reference point for fast-talking comedy, from Gilmore Girls to Aaron Sorkin's entire career.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use — renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case. This one has an extra layer: the film is adapted from the stage play "The Front Page" (Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur), whose own separate copyright didn't expire until 2024 — the film itself lapsed decades earlier, but the underlying play was a distinct rights question until recently.

films.title: Night of the Living Dead
films.scene_description: Johnny mock-scares his sister with "They're coming to get you, Barbara" moments before the film's first real attack.
films.commentary: Romero shot this on a shoestring in rural Pennsylvania, and the grainy 16mm newsreel look wasn't a style choice — it's just what a $114,000 budget gets you. That accidental realism is what made it terrifying. It also invented the modern zombie outright; the word "zombie" never appears in the script.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain immediately upon release because the distributor's title-card change dropped the copyright notice, which US law at the time required.

films.title: Metropolis
films.scene_description: The robot double of Maria is brought to life in rings of light.
films.commentary: This transformation was built with practical light rings and in-camera exposure tricks decades before CGI existed — nobody has fully reverse-engineered Lang's exact method. The robot itself became the template for basically every sci-fi android after it, C-3PO included. A hundred years old and it still looks expensive.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired for the original 1927 release (published well past the 95-year term).
films.pd_caveat: The only prints readily available are the 2010 "complete" restoration, which adds newly rediscovered footage of its own. This clip is limited to the robot-transformation shot specifically, which was already present in every prior public-domain cut — a plain rescan of pre-existing PD frames is unlikely to carry its own copyright, but confirm before commercial use, and avoid pulling clips from this print's newly-restored scenes.

films.title: A Trip to the Moon
films.scene_description: The capsule strikes the anthropomorphic Man in the Moon squarely in the eye — cinema's first iconic special-effects image.
films.commentary: Méliès gets this effect with nothing but a papier-mâché moon and his signature stop-substitution splice — a trick he stumbled into by accident years earlier when his camera jammed mid-shot on a Paris street. It's the first special-effects image anyone still remembers, reproduced for over a century, from posters to a Smashing Pumpkins video.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1902, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Safety Last!
films.scene_description: Harold Lloyd dangles from the hands of a giant clock face, high above a real city street.
films.commentary: Lloyd was missing most of his right hand from a prop-bomb accident three years earlier and wore a prosthetic glove to hide it through every one of these climbs. The buildings were staged in forced perspective on rooftops with a mattress-covered platform just out of camera range — real height, real risk, no trick photography for the fall itself.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1923, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Phantom of the Opera
films.scene_description: Christine pulls the mask from Erik's face, revealing the skull-like makeup underneath in a long, unflinching close-up.
films.commentary: Lon Chaney designed and applied this makeup himself, using wire to flare his nostrils and paint to hollow out his eyes and cheekbones. Universal kept the unmasked face out of all pre-release publicity specifically so 1925 audiences would see it for the first time in the theater, screaming right along with Christine.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Kid
films.scene_description: The Tramp sprints across rooftops between chimneys, a policeman right behind him, racing to catch the orphanage truck taking the boy away.
films.commentary: Chaplin shot this the same year he was fighting to keep the film out of a bankruptcy settlement entirely, re-editing it in secret and smuggling the negative to Utah in a fruit truck. The chase reads as pure slapstick, but it comes right after a scene of the Tramp genuinely sobbing on a doorstep -- the tonal whiplash was the whole point.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1921, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: White Zombie
films.scene_description: At her own wedding dinner, Madeleine drinks from a goblet Legendre poisoned -- his glowing, superimposed eyes and face appear inside the glass as the mesmeric hold takes effect.
films.commentary: Bela Lugosi's eyes were double-exposed directly into the wine glass for this shot -- the first feature film built entirely around Haitian zombie folklore, sixteen years before the word reached Val Lewton or Romero. Legendre's poisoned toast and the stare that follows became the single image most associated with the movie, reprinted on posters long after the film itself nearly vanished from circulation.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Häxan
films.scene_description: Dramatizing a confessed witch's testimony, silhouetted figures fly by broomstick through the night sky toward a towering, horned devil waiting on the mountain.
films.commentary: Christensen shot this as a direct illustration of real interrogation transcripts -- the intertitle quotes an actual confession about flying to Blockula on a neighbor's broom. Equal parts silent horror film and lecture on medieval psychiatry, it was banned outright in the US for years and remains one of the most explicit silent films ever made about what accused witches were tortured into "confessing."
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1922, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Reefer Madness
films.scene_description: At a house party, a young man newly hooked on marijuana pounds out a wild, unhinged piece at the piano while a woman claws at him, the scene building toward the film's most infamous freak-out.
films.commentary: Financed by a church group as a straight-faced morality tale, this scene is the reason the film survives at all: decades after its warnings stopped scaring anyone, midnight-movie and college audiences of the 1970s embraced it as unintentional comedy, and it's been in constant circulation ever since. The propaganda failed completely; the piano scene became immortal anyway.
films.pd_basis: Copyright was never renewed, and multiple sources indicate the film may have entered the public domain even earlier due to a defective or missing original notice -- either way it's one of the most-cited public-domain films in the US.
films.pd_caveat: Widely treated as public domain and freely redistributed for decades, but exact chain-of-title research varies by source -- confirm before commercial use.

films.title: The Great Train Robbery
films.scene_label: The gunman fires at the audience
films.scene_description: In a shot with no connection to the plot, an outlaw raises his revolver, aims it straight at the camera, and fires -- the first time a film ever pointed a gun directly at its own audience.
films.commentary: Exhibitors could splice this shot at the start of the reel or the end, and many chose the end so the film closed on it -- 1903 audiences reportedly screamed or ducked, since no one had ever been aimed at by a movie before. It's the moment film editing discovered it could touch the viewer, not just show them something, and it kicked off the Western as a genre in the same twelve minutes.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1903, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Detour
films.scene_description: Al drags a telephone cord under a locked door in a blind rage, not realizing it's wrapped around Vera's neck on the other side -- one of noir's most infamous accidental murders, shot almost entirely through a closed door.
films.commentary: Shot in about six days for roughly $20,000 by a Poverty Row studio, Detour turns its own cheapness into style -- fog, shadow, and a murder the hero insists was just bad luck. Al narrates the whole film as a man fate keeps tripping, and this scene is the moment the audience has to decide whether to believe him. It's since been restored by the Academy Film Archive and inducted into the National Film Registry.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Charade
films.scene_description: At a stiffly formal Paris viewing, a coroner leans deep into the open casket to double-check the corpse -- and the row of black-veiled mourners, Audrey Hepburn among them, react in unison.
films.commentary: Cary Grant and Audrey Hepburn's glossy studio thriller opens its story with this scene played almost entirely for black comedy, which is the whole trick of Charade: it's routinely called the best Hitchcock movie Hitchcock never made, mixing real menace with genuine wit. Big stars, a major studio, and a real box-office hit -- and it landed in the public domain anyway, which surprises almost everyone who hears it.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain immediately upon release because the film's copyright notice omitted the required word or symbol ("Copyright", "Copr.", or ©), which US law at the time required.

films.title: The Unknown
films.scene_description: Nanon, strapped spread-eagled against a target board in front of a carnival crowd, waits as Alonzo -- billed as armless -- lines up to fire at her using only his feet.
films.commentary: Lon Chaney kept his arms bound to his torso for months to play Alonzo convincingly, in a performance built entirely around a secret the plot keeps twisting: Alonzo isn't really armless, and that lie is what eventually drives him to demand actual, surgical self-mutilation later in the film. It's one of silent horror's most disturbing love stories, and one of the earliest films to give a young Joan Crawford real screen presence.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1927, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
films.scene_description: Jekyll drinks his own untested formula, and Hyde emerges through nothing but Barrymore's posture and facial contortion -- no cut, no makeup change, no trick photography.
films.commentary: John Barrymore did his own first transformation with zero special effects, hunching and twisting his face into Hyde live in front of the camera; the makeup only got more elaborate in later scenes, once the character had further to fall. Often called the first great American horror film, it set the template every Jekyll-and-Hyde adaptation since has been measured against.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Cocaine Fiends
films.scene_description: Alone by a steaming radiator, a young woman hooked on cocaine grips her own arms, wracked with need, unable to sit still.
films.commentary: A remake of the 1928 silent The Pace That Kills, this is close to the direct template Reefer Madness copied a year later -- roadshow drug-scare pictures were their own little genre, shot cheap and fast for theaters that toured them town to town outside the regular studio system. It's melodrama, not medicine, but the panic it's selling became a genuine cultural template.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: My Man Godfrey
films.scene_description: At a Depression-era society scavenger hunt, a Park Avenue socialite in a sequined gown finds her prize item at the city dump: a 'forgotten man.'
films.commentary: The joke -- rich people turning homeless men into a party game -- was sharp enough in 1936 that the film still reads as social commentary, not just farce, underneath the screwball banter. William Powell and Carole Lombard, married and divorced in real life by the time they made this together, have a chemistry the studio bet the whole picture on. It was nominated for six Oscars and lost every one, and is still one of the genre's high points.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Pandora's Box
films.scene_description: In a bare London room on Christmas Eve, a stranger's hand closes around a knife on the table -- Lulu's final admirer isn't who he seems.
films.commentary: Pabst cast an American unknown, Louise Brooks, over every established German star being considered, and her performance as Lulu -- pure appetite, no shame about it, destroyed by a world that punishes women for exactly that -- is still the reason the film is discussed today. This closing scene identifies her killer only by implication; German censors of the era wouldn't allow his name spoken outright, but everyone in 1929 knew exactly who was in the room with her.
films.pd_basis: Never registered for US copyright and not renewed; entered the public domain in the US as an unregistered foreign work.
films.pd_caveat: Foreign-film PD status under the US's URAA rules turns on registration and renewal history that can be genuinely hard to verify -- confirm independently before commercial use.

films.title: The Phantom Carriage
films.scene_description: A hooded figure kneels by a skeletal horse and cart at the edge of a cemetery, both rendered as ghostly double exposures -- whoever dies last each year must drive Death's carriage for the next.
films.commentary: Sjöström shot the same footage twice and combined it in-camera to get this translucent, layered ghost effect -- no opticals, no lab tricks available yet in 1921, just precise double exposure. Ingmar Bergman called it one of the films that made him want to make films at all, and screened it every year on his birthday for most of his life; the hooded Death figure here is a direct ancestor of Bergman's own in The Seventh Seal.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1921, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Steamboat Willie
films.scene_description: During the barnyard 'Turkey in the Straw' number, Mickey Mouse plays a cow's bared teeth like a xylophone, mallets in hand.
films.commentary: Steamboat Willie wasn't Mickey's first cartoon, but it was the first released with synchronized sound, and the one that made him a star. On January 1, 2024, its copyright expired after exactly 95 years -- one of the most publicized public domain days ever, with news outlets worldwide covering the moment this specific film, and only this one, became free to use.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1928, well past the 95-year term).
films.pd_caveat: The film's copyright is fully expired, but Disney still holds trademark rights over the Mickey Mouse character -- solid ground for hosting this original 1928 short itself, but worth knowing before building anything derivative from the character.

films.title: Battleship Potemkin
films.scene_description: A mother collapses on the Odessa steps as Cossack soldiers fire into a fleeing crowd, her baby carriage left teetering at the top -- moments before it begins rolling down the stairs alone.
films.commentary: The massacre on the steps never actually happened -- Eisenstein invented it for the film -- but the sequence's editing rhythm is so influential it's taught in nearly every film school on earth, and its unattended-carriage-rolling-downstairs image has been directly restaged in everything from The Untouchables to Naked Gun 33 1/3. Montage editing as a technique essentially starts here.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Nanook of the North
films.scene_description: Nanook cuts and stacks blocks of snow by hand, raising the walls of a winter igloo alone on the open ice.
films.commentary: Widely credited as the first commercially successful feature-length documentary, though 'documentary' undersells how staged it was: the man billed as Nanook was really Allakariallak, some of the hunting techniques shown had already been abandoned in favor of rifles, and Flaherty had his cast re-enact a version of traditional life for the camera. It's still one of the founding arguments in an argument documentary filmmaking has never fully settled -- how much reconstruction a 'true' record can contain.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1922, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Un Chien Andalou
films.scene_label: Prologue: the razor and the moon
films.scene_description: The film's prologue: a man gazes up at a cloud sliding across the moon, then turns to a woman, pins her eye open with his fingers, and brings a straight razor to it -- caught here in the instant before the cut that made the film infamous.
films.commentary: A 16-minute collaboration between Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, built from dream logic rather than plot -- ants crawling from a hand, a severed hand in the street, a man dragging two grand pianos loaded with dead donkeys. None of it outlasted the opening image: a straight razor drawn across an open eye, cut together with a cloud slicing the moon so the audience's mind does the cutting for it. (The eye belonged to a calf, not the actress -- a substitution convincing enough that it's still routinely mistaken for real.) It became the founding text of surrealist cinema and one of the most analyzed sixteen minutes in film history.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1929, well past the 95-year term).
films.pd_caveat: As a foreign work, it also had to clear registration and renewal formalities that don't apply to US productions -- Internet Archive's own curators only cleared it for US public domain in January 2025. It remains under copyright in Spain, its country of origin, until 2060.

films.title: Maniac
films.scene_label: “Not unlike an oyster, or a grape”
films.scene_description: Alone in the lab and unraveling inside his stolen identity, Maxwell holds something small up to the light, admires it, then tips his head back and swallows -- the beat that made this obscure grindhouse picture a genre-history footnote.
films.commentary: Dwain Esper built a career selling lurid B-pictures as public-health warnings, padding each one with fake “educational” title cards on mental illness to dodge obscenity laws while delivering exactly the shock content the cards claimed to warn against. Maniac -- a barely-coherent riff on Poe's “The Black Cat” and “Murders in the Rue Morgue” -- is the most notorious example: a deranged Maxwell, hiding inside the identity of the mad scientist he murdered, catches a cat and eats its eye. Film historians generally agree the eye was a rigged prop rather than a real animal's, but the scene became exploitation cinema's most cited party trick regardless.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Tomorrow's Children
films.scene_description: A nurse rushes in with an urgent warning as surgeons gather around a draped operating table and gloved hands close in with an instrument -- the forced sterilization the whole film has been racing to stop, caught here at its most tense.
films.commentary: By the early 1930s, more than half of US states had eugenics laws on the books, and tens of thousands of Americans -- prisoners, psychiatric patients, the poor -- had been forcibly sterilized under them, a practice the Supreme Court upheld in Buck v. Bell (“three generations of imbeciles are enough,” Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote for the majority). Tomorrow's Children turned that policy into a ticking-clock melodrama: a seventeen-year-old ordered sterilized because of her parents' problems, and a race to stop the surgeons before it's too late. The filmmaking is clumsy, but the target was real, and versions of the law it argues against stayed on the books in some states into the 1970s.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: D.O.A.
films.scene_label: I want to report a murder
films.scene_description: Bigelow walks into the police homicide division, and when the detective asks who was murdered, delivers the line that gives the film its title -- a walking dead man narrating the case of his own poisoning.
films.commentary: D.O.A. opens with its whole premise front-loaded: Frank Bigelow, poisoned with a slow-acting toxin he can't survive, spends the rest of the film investigating who killed him and why, racing a clock that's already run out. Edmond O'Brien plays the reveal completely straight, delivering "I want to report a murder... mine" without a wink, and the gambit worked well enough that the fatally-poisoned-man setup has been recycled by a stage musical, a 1969 West German remake, a 1988 Dennis Quaid version, and a 2022 reboot -- none of which needed permission, since the original fell into the public domain decades ago.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: Beat the Devil
films.scene_label: The gang can't stop laughing at themselves
films.scene_description: Peterson and his fellow schemers, holed up plotting their next move, dissolve into helpless laughter at their own scheme -- the loose, improvisational comic tone the whole film runs on.
films.commentary: Beat the Devil was written day-by-day during shooting -- John Huston and a 29-year-old Truman Capote reworking pages each morning for that day's scenes, with Humphrey Bogart (who co-produced and financed it) reportedly baffled by what the finished film was even supposed to be. Contemporary audiences mostly agreed, and it flopped; decades later it's better understood as an early spoof of the prestige-thriller genre Bogart himself helped define, deadpan enough that people still argue about which lines are meant to be jokes.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Renewal-lapse titles like this one are well documented, but always confirm current status before commercial use -- renewal research is more error-prone than a straightforward term-expiration case.

films.title: The Little Shop of Horrors
films.scene_description: Seymour, sent to pull a tooth so his carnivorous plant has something to eat, tries to bolt from the dentist's chair -- the two end up wrestling around the office instead.
films.commentary: Roger Corman shot the entire film in two days and a night on sets left over from another production, mostly to test how fast a feature could be made on a bet. He never bothered securing the copyright, evidently not expecting it to have value beyond a quick theatrical run -- which is exactly why it's free to use today, while the 1986 musical remake it inspired stayed firmly copyrighted. This dental-office scene is also where a 23-year-old Jack Nicholson turns up in one of his first film roles, as the patient who shows up next and can't wait for his turn in the chair.
films.pd_basis: Entered the public domain when its US copyright registration was not renewed at the required 28-year mark.
films.pd_caveat: Some sources instead say the film was never formally copyrighted at all -- either way, it's one of the most widely cited and freely redistributed public-domain films in the US, but confirm current status before commercial use.

films.title: Steamboat Bill, Jr.
films.scene_description: As a cyclone tears through town, Buster stands motionless in the exact spot where a collapsing house's attic window will pass clean over him -- the whole two-story facade crashes down around him, missing him by inches on every side.
films.commentary: The falling building front weighed about two tons, and the attic window was sized to clear Keaton's body by only a few inches on either side -- the crew reportedly couldn't bear to watch, and Keaton insisted on doing the stunt himself, marking his exact spot on the ground beforehand. There was no trick photography: one camera, one take, and a genuinely lethal margin for error if the wind had pushed the facade even slightly off its rig. It's routinely cited as the single most dangerous shot of the silent era, and stunt coordinators still study it today.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1928, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Sherlock Jr.
films.scene_description: Having fallen asleep as the theater's projectionist, Buster's dream-self wanders down the aisle and into the screen, and the backdrop keeps cutting out from under him -- a desert one moment, a rock in the middle of the ocean the next.
films.commentary: Getting Keaton to appear seamlessly inside a rapid series of environments -- a desert, a busy street, a mountain ledge, the open ocean -- required none of the compositing tools that would later make this kind of effect routine; in 1924 it meant surveying each location in advance, chalking Keaton's exact mark, and matching the camera's height, distance, and lens precisely between setups so the cut from one world to the next would land as a jolt instead of an obvious scene change. It's still cited as one of the most technically demanding effects sequences of the silent era, achieved with nothing but a tape measure and exact repetition.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1924, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Hunchback of Notre Dame
films.scene_description: Quasimodo scales down the cathedral's ornate facade to snatch Esmeralda from the gallows below, then carries her inside Notre Dame -- under medieval law, once she's within its walls, the church itself becomes her only protection from execution.
films.commentary: Universal built a full-scale reproduction of the Notre Dame plaza on its studio lot -- reportedly the most expensive set built in Hollywood up to that point -- and populated it with thousands of extras for the film's climactic siege. Lon Chaney designed and built his own Quasimodo makeup and body rig, including a twenty-to-thirty-pound rubber hump and harness he wore through the entire shoot in the California sun. The "sanctuary" the film's plot hinges on was real medieval law: a church genuinely could shelter a fugitive from secular arrest, at least temporarily, and that specific legal technicality is what the climax turns on.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1923, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Lost World
films.scene_description: The expedition's captured brontosaurus breaks loose from its crane cage on the London docks and stampedes through the city, flattening buildings before vanishing into the Thames.
films.commentary: Willis O'Brien's stop-motion effects here were the first time mass audiences had seen dinosaurs move and interact with a live-action world at this scale, and the techniques he refined -- posable armature models, incremental frame-by-frame animation, miniatures matted into real footage -- became the direct blueprint for his own King Kong eight years later. Three years before the film even opened, Arthur Conan Doyle previewed O'Brien's test reel -- a Triceratops family, an Allosaurus attack, a Stegosaurus -- for a room of magicians that included Harry Houdini, coyly calling the creatures "psychic" and letting the room debate whether they'd just watched something real. In 1998 the Library of Congress added the finished film to the National Film Registry.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed
films.scene_label: The stolen flying horse takes off
films.scene_description: Prince Achmed steals a sorcerer's magic mechanical horse and, working out its controls mid-flight, sends it rearing up over the palace and out across the rooftops.
films.commentary: Every figure on screen is a hand-cut, hinged cardboard-and-lead-foil silhouette, animated a fraction of a millimeter at a time and shot frame by frame in a friend's garage by a crew of five. To fake real depth, Reiniger stacked her silhouettes across horizontal panes of glass at different distances from the camera and moved them independently -- a multiplane setup she worked out roughly a decade before Walt Disney's studio patented and popularized its own version. The film took about five years to complete. Because the two earlier animated features by Quirino Cristiani in Argentina no longer survive, Prince Achmed stands as the oldest surviving animated feature film.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Faust
films.scene_label: Mephisto's wings blot out the sky
films.scene_description: Answering Satan's wager that he can corrupt one righteous soul, Mephisto spreads his wings over Faust's home town, and plague spreads wherever their shadow falls.
films.commentary: The village beneath Mephisto's wings is a miniature model, not a full-size set -- art director Robert Herlth's team built it from reeds and rushes standing in for pine trees, glass wool for clouds, and real turf glued onto plaster, with the buildings' proportions deliberately warped to read as vast, crooked distance under the demon's shadow. Emil Jannings plays Mephisto here, a few years before he'd move to Hollywood and become the first person to win the Academy Award for Best Actor, for two other films. Murnau himself considered the picture troubled -- he reshot the ending after a poor test screening -- but this looming apparition over the model village became one of the most reproduced single images of the silent era.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Thief of Bagdad
films.scene_label: The flying carpet, and the Princess
films.scene_description: Ahmed reunites with the Princess on the magic carpet as it carries them to safety over a Bagdad seized by the Mongol army.
films.commentary: The bazaar set alone covered more than two acres on a concrete floor that had to be re-enameled several times a week, part of a production budget over $1.1 million -- an enormous sum for 1924 -- under design chief William Cameron Menzies, whose soaring, geometric sets here launched his career and helped invent what the industry would later call production design. Filming ran more than 28 weeks. Douglas Fairbanks, who produced and starred, did his own stunts and insisted on practical in-camera effects for the flying carpet and the rest of the film's magic rather than the optical trickery available at the time.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1924, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Mark of Zorro
films.scene_description: Recognizing Zorro's swordplay from an earlier duel, the villain finally faces the masked avenger blade to blade.
films.commentary: Adapted from Johnston McCulley's pulp serial "The Curse of Capistrano," this was Fairbanks's first costume swashbuckler after a decade of contemporary comedies, and its success reoriented the rest of his career toward the swordfights and derring-do he's remembered for. Fairbanks did the bulk of his own stunt work and fencing here, athletic enough that decades later Bob Kane cited this exact film -- the mask, the cape, the double identity of a foppish nobleman hiding a masked vigilante -- as a direct model for Batman.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Body and Soul
films.scene_description: In his screen debut, Paul Robeson plays a false preacher working his congregation, opening a sermon before a room that doesn't yet see through him.
films.commentary: This was Paul Robeson's first film role, and he plays two parts -- the corrupt "Reverend" seen here, and that man's honest twin brother -- a dual performance Micheaux built the entire film around. Micheaux wrote, directed, produced, and distributed the picture independently outside the studio system, one of the so-called "race films" made explicitly for Black audiences at a time when most American theaters were segregated. New York's censors found its portrait of a fraudulent preacher offensive enough that they forced Micheaux to cut the original nine-reel version down to five before it could screen at all; that shortened cut is the only version known to survive.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Black Pirate
films.scene_description: The pirate captain plunges his knife into the topsail and rides it down to the deck, tearing the canvas in half as he falls.
films.commentary: The stunt was faked, brilliantly: the sail was pre-slit, Fairbanks gripped a fixed blade rigged to a hidden pulley-and-counterbalance system his own brother Robert engineered, and his weight on the rig lowered him smoothly to the deck while the canvas tore open around him -- airplane propellers off camera billowed the sails for effect. It's also one of the very first color feature films: shot entirely in an early two-strip Technicolor process, only the third feature ever to use it, requiring two strips of film fused back-to-back, so thick and heat-sensitive the picture would warp out of focus during projection. Fairbanks, in his forties by then, still did the stunt work himself, taping his arms and legs to avoid rope burns.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Salomé
films.scene_label: The Dance of the Seven Veils
films.scene_description: Salomé dances for her stepfather Herod, the price of the dance being anything she desires -- including, she has already decided, the head of the prophet who spurned her.
films.commentary: Alla Nazimova produced this herself and, though her husband Charles Bryant received the director's credit, most who worked on it -- and most historians since -- consider Nazimova its real director. A persistent rumor holds she cast the entire production with gay and bisexual performers as a tribute to Oscar Wilde; one extra later said gay cast members were indeed present, just not an unusual number of them, let alone all. Costume and set designer Natacha Rambova built every frame directly from Aubrey Beardsley's scandalous 1890s illustrations for Wilde's play -- the film's own opening credits bill her work as "after Aubrey Beardsley." It flopped on release and effectively ended Nazimova's career as a major studio star; it's since been reclaimed as a cult classic.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1923, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Traffic in Souls
films.scene_description: Police interrupt a formal engagement party to arrest the ring's respectable-seeming financier, armed with recordings his own target's father secretly made of his voice.
films.commentary: Made for about $5,700 and grossing roughly $450,000, this was the film that established Universal as a major studio. Its plot turns on an early piece of surveillance fiction: the missing girl's father, a deaf inventor, has built a phonographic recording device, and his daughter uses it to secretly capture the trafficking ring's own voices as evidence against them. Marketed as an exposé of the real "white slavery" panic gripping American cities at the time, it was a sensation on release, drawing both audiences and moral reformers -- one of the earliest American feature films built explicitly as a message picture. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2006.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1913, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Intolerance
films.scene_description: In the film's ancient-Babylon strand, worshippers crowd the base of the city's colossal winged-bull gods -- one of four separate historical eras Griffith crosscuts between across the film's three-hour runtime.
films.commentary: Griffith built this Babylon set to a scale nothing in film had attempted before -- walls and towering statuary reportedly visible for miles across Hollywood, populated with some 3,000 extras for its crowd scenes, standing for years afterward as a local landmark before it was finally torn down. He made the film partly as his answer to the firestorm of criticism over his previous picture, The Birth of a Nation: an epic about the destructive cost of intolerance across four different eras of history, crosscut together in a way virtually no one had tried at feature length before. It was a costly commercial failure on release and contributed to Griffith's later financial troubles, but its editing techniques went on to influence nearly every filmmaker who saw it.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1916, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Way Down East
films.scene_description: Stranded unconscious on a breaking ice floe drifting toward a waterfall, Anna is reached just in time by the man who loves her, leaping floe to floe to carry her to shore.
films.commentary: Lillian Gish did her own stunts here, no double, on real breaking ice during a New England blizzard in temperatures below zero -- about twenty takes a day for three weeks left her with frostbitten fingers and nerve damage in the hand she trailed in the freezing water, feeling she said she never fully got back. Griffith himself was frostbitten on one side of his face directing the scene. Gish had spent the weeks beforehand taking daily ice baths and walking the streets coatless to prepare her body for the cold. None of it was faked: the ice really was breaking apart under them as the cameras rolled.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: A Fool There Was
films.scene_description: The Vampire closes in on the married diplomat she's chosen to destroy, delivering the line that would become the film's most quoted, and most imitated, moment.
films.commentary: Theda Bara plays "The Vampire" -- never given an actual name -- and the film made her one of the first manufactured movie stars, complete with a fabricated backstory claiming she was born in the shadow of the Sphinx to a French artist and an Arabian princess (she was actually from Cincinnati). Its intertitle "Kiss me, my fool!" became one of the most quoted lines of the silent era, endlessly repeated and misquoted as "kiss me, you fool" for decades after. The film adapts a 1909 Broadway play, itself inspired by Rudyard Kipling's poem "The Vampire," and it's largely responsible for popularizing the word "vamp" as shorthand for a seductive femme fatale.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1915, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Golem: How He Came into the World
films.scene_description: Rabbi Loew slides the star-shaped amulet, engraved with the magic word AEMAET, into the clay figure's chest. A beat of stillness, then an extreme close-up: the Golem's stone eyes snap open.
films.commentary: Paul Wegener not only co-directed but plays the Golem himself, under makeup and a heavy clay-textured suit designed by Expressionist architect Hans Poelzig. The film is a prequel to two earlier Golem films Wegener had already made and lost, and it's the one that survives complete. Its blocky, jagged medieval-ghetto sets and the Golem's own lumbering, silent menace fed directly into Hollywood horror a decade later -- Boris Karloff's Frankenstein's Monster owes a visible debt to Wegener's performance and silhouette.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1920, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life
films.director: Merian C. Cooper, Ernest B. Schoedsack
films.scene_description: A single-file line of pack animals and tribespeople, silhouetted against jagged peaks, claws its way up a steep, snow-choked mountainside during the Bakhtiari's twice-yearly migration.
films.commentary: Cooper and Schoedsack shot this with no actors, no script, and barely any budget, following the Bakhtiari people of Persia on their real, brutal migration over the Zagros Mountains in search of grazing land -- fording an icy river and then climbing an near-vertical, snowbound pass, on foot, with their herds. The two filmmakers were so taken with adventure filmmaking after this that they went on to make King Kong together eight years later. Grass is now preserved in the National Film Registry as one of the earliest feature-length documentaries.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog
films.scene_description: A fog-wreathed figure appears at the boarding-house door asking for a room, his face wrapped in a scarf to the eyes. The landlady looks up at him, framed from below on the staircase, unsure what she's just let in.
films.commentary: Hitchcock always called this his first true film -- the first to show "the Hitchcock touch." He was 27, working from a novel loosely inspired by Jack the Ripper, and already reaching for the visual tricks that would define his career: a glass floor built into the set so the camera could look straight up through the ceiling at the lodger's pacing feet, and a wrongly-suspected man at the center of the plot, a theme Hitchcock would return to again and again over the next five decades. Star Ivor Novello was already a matinee idol, which forced the studio to soften the ending so its heartthrob couldn't turn out to be the killer.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1927, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Gertie the Dinosaur
films.scene_label: "Be a good girl and bow to the audience."
films.scene_description: Gertie the Brontosaurus, coaxed by her off-screen animator, dips her long neck all the way to the ground in a big, showy bow for the crowd.
films.commentary: McCay, already famous for the comic strip Little Nemo, hand-drew every one of Gertie's roughly 10,000 frames himself and originally performed the film live on vaudeville stages, standing beside the screen with a whip, "commanding" Gertie to bow, dance, and cry on cue as if she were really responding to him. She was the first animated character ever given a distinct, appealing personality rather than just a gag-delivery device, which makes Gertie the direct ancestor of every cartoon character with a face audiences actually cared about, from Mickey Mouse onward.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1914, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Iron Horse
films.scene_label: The Golden Spike at Promontory Point
films.scene_description: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific locomotives roll nose to nose as a huge crowd packs the gap between them -- a careful recreation of the famous 1869 photograph marking the completion of America's first transcontinental railroad.
films.commentary: This was John Ford's first big-budget epic, made when he was still in his twenties, and Fox threw real resources at it: thousands of extras, cavalry, Chinese and Irish laborers, herds of buffalo, and two replica locomotives built to match the original Jupiter and No. 119 engines down to the rivets. Ford shot much of it on location in the Nevada desert in brutal winter conditions, and the finished film helped define the Western epic as a genre a full generation before Ford's own Stagecoach.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1924, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Wings
films.scene_description: A German patrol dives out of the clouds, wingtips crossing just past the camera, as the pilot's-eye view puts the audience right in the cockpit for the attack.
films.commentary: Wings won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Picture and remains the only fully silent film to do so. Director William Wellman, a World War I combat pilot himself, insisted on shooting real aerial combat with cameras mounted directly on the planes rather than using models, which meant training his stars, including Clara Bow and a young, then-unknown Gary Cooper in a small early role, to fly. The production borrowed actual Army Air Corps pilots and aircraft, and several stunt fliers were injured during filming chasing shots no one had attempted before.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1927, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Covered Wagon
films.scene_description: A mile-long wagon train drives its oxen teams straight into the rushing river, wagon after wagon fighting the current as riders wade alongside to keep the herd moving.
films.commentary: The Covered Wagon was the picture that proved the Western could be an event, not just a two-reel programmer. Paramount sent director James Cruze and a full production unit deep into Utah and Nevada to shoot with real wagon trains, real livestock, and hundreds of extras fording an actual river rather than a studio tank, and audiences in 1923 had never seen anything like it. It became one of the biggest box-office hits of the silent era and set the template every big-budget Western since, from Wagon Master to Red River, has followed.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1923, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: The Big Parade
films.scene_label: Melisande runs for the departing truck
films.scene_description: As the convoy pulls out for the front, Melisande breaks from the crowd and sprints alongside James's truck, grabbing for the tailgate and being dragged along rather than let go.
films.commentary: The Big Parade was the film that made King Vidor a top-tier director and John Gilbert a superstar, and it stayed MGM's highest-grossing silent picture for years. Vidor shot the farewell sequence, a French village girl clinging to a departing supply truck as her soldier sweetheart is hauled away to the front, almost entirely with actors and extras rather than trick photography, and it became one of the most reproduced images of the silent era. The film's unsentimental battle scenes, filmed with Army cooperation and real veterans as extras, were as influential on later war pictures as its romance was on every farewell scene that followed.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Frankenstein
films.scene_description: Inside a bubbling vat, a smoking, skeletal mass gradually builds itself into a full humanoid form, arms reaching up through the smoke as it comes to life.
films.commentary: This is the first-ever film adaptation of Frankenstein, made by Thomas Edison's own studio just twelve years after cinema itself was born. Director J. Searle Dawley created the monster's creation scene by burning a papier-mache dummy in a controlled fire and filming it, then running that footage in reverse, so the creature appears to assemble itself out of smoke and flame rather than fall apart. It's one of the earliest documented in-camera special effects in film history, and the only surviving print for decades was a private collector's copy, not rediscovered by the public until the 1970s.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1910, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: He Who Gets Slapped
films.scene_description: In close-up, the circus clown known only as HE braces as a fellow performer's open hand connects across his painted face, the crowd roaring with laughter in the stands behind him.
films.commentary: He Who Gets Slapped was the very first film released by the newly formed Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, and it made Lon Chaney one of the studio's defining stars before he ever put on the makeup he's best remembered for. Chaney plays a humiliated scientist who reinvents himself as a circus clown whose entire act is being slapped in the face by his fellow performers while the audience howls, a running bit that Chaney plays as pure showmanship on the surface and quiet devastation underneath. The image of the laughing-on-the-outside tragic clown, endlessly reproduced since, traces directly back to this performance.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1924, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Seven Chances
films.scene_description: Sprinting full-tilt down a steep hillside, Jimmie dodges a barrage of massive boulders that tumble after him, one grazing past his shoulder as he weaves and stumbles to stay ahead of it.
films.commentary: Seven Chances closes with one of the most celebrated physical sequences in silent comedy: Buster Keaton, fleeing an ever-growing mob, stumbles into a real avalanche of boulders and has to outrun them down an actual hillside. Keaton did the stunt himself with no safety rigging, dodging a mix of real rocks and oversized papier-mache boulders built to roll convincingly at speed, and the sequence was reportedly added only after a test screening got a bigger laugh from an accidental rockslide than anything else in the film. It's been cited by directors from Jackie Chan to Edgar Wright as a benchmark for what practical stunt comedy can do.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1925, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Man with a Movie Camera
films.scene_label: The cameraman atop his own camera
films.scene_description: A tiny cameraman stands cranking his tripod-mounted camera while perched directly on top of an enormous superimposed movie camera, a surreal double-exposure announcing the film's obsession with the mechanics of seeing.
films.commentary: Man with a Movie Camera is a city-symphony documentary with no actors, no sets, and no intertitles, built entirely from a single day in Soviet urban life and Dziga Vertov's belief that the camera could see truth the human eye couldn't. This opening image, a cameraman dwarfed atop his own giant apparatus, announces the film's constant self-awareness: it shows its own editor at work, its own audience watching it, and its own camera being carried into traffic and up factory scaffolding to get the shot. It topped Sight & Sound's directors' and critics' polls decades later as one of the greatest documentaries ever made.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1929, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Cabiria
films.scene_description: An armored war elephant, draped in a covered howdah, picks its way through a snowbound mountain pass as Hannibal's army streams across the ridgeline behind it.
films.commentary: Cabiria was the era's defining spectacle picture, an internationally distributed sensation that directly shaped D.W. Griffith's Intolerance and set the template for every 'cast of thousands' epic that followed. Director Giovanni Pastrone staged Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with real elephants and hundreds of extras on an actual mountainside rather than a studio backlot, and the film's title cards were reportedly the first to credit a poet, Gabriele D'Annunzio, giving the production literary prestige it used to market itself worldwide. It also introduced Maciste, one of cinema's first recurring action heroes, who went on to star in dozens of his own films.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1914, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Aelita: Queen of Mars
films.scene_description: Beneath jagged Constructivist arches, robed Martian courtiers line a vast stepped amphitheater as a figure in an angular, wing-spiked costume descends the stairs into their midst.
films.commentary: Aelita: Queen of Mars was Soviet cinema's first venture into science fiction, built around a Martian civilization designed by Constructivist artist Alexandra Exter, whose jutting geometric sets and armor-plated costumes drew directly on Cubist and Suprematist theory rather than anything from earlier fantasy filmmaking. The angular, alien production design is frequently cited as a direct visual precursor to Metropolis, released three years later. Its box-office success made the queen played by Yuliya Solntseva, an enduring image of Soviet-era science fiction, reproduced on posters and book covers for decades after.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1924, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Gulliver's Travels
films.scene_label: Staked to the beach by the Lilliputians
films.scene_description: Gulliver lies asleep under a starry sky, pinned to the sand by dozens of ropes as an army of tiny torch-bearing Lilliputians swarm across his enormous body.
films.commentary: Gulliver's Travels was Fleischer Studios' answer to Disney's Snow White, and only the second animated feature ever released, rushed into production specifically to prove Max and Dave Fleischer could compete at feature length. The waking-on-the-beach sequence, Gulliver dwarfing an entire kingdom's worth of tiny staked-down ropes, became the single most reproduced image from the film and the one most audiences still remember. Its copyright was never renewed at the required interval, a lapse that also freed Popeye and Superman's earliest Fleischer cartoons decades later, though this is the studio's only full animated feature to fall into the public domain this way.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired via non-renewal (published 1939; the required renewal filing was never made).

films.title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
films.scene_description: Asked whether the voice she heard had long hair, Joan's face fills the frame in unbroken close-up, eyes glistening as she looks upward, unflinching under the judges' questioning.
films.commentary: The Passion of Joan of Arc is built almost entirely out of faces in extreme close-up, an approach so radical for 1928 that Carl Dreyer had sets built and then largely refused to show them, trusting Renee Jeanne Falconetti's performance to carry the film alone. She reportedly never acted again after this role, and film historians still debate how much of her visible anguish was performance versus Dreyer's famously punishing directing methods. The film was thought lost for decades until a nearly pristine print turned up in a Norwegian mental institution's closet in 1981.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1928, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: A Page of Madness
films.scene_label: The dancer against the striped drum
films.scene_description: A woman in a flowing white dress spins and reaches beside a huge striped drum, a jagged lightning-bolt backdrop behind her, in one of the film's stylized reverie sequences.
films.commentary: A Page of Madness has no intertitles at all, telling its story entirely through Teinosuke Kinugasa's rapid-fire editing, double exposures, and expressionist staging, a technique closer to European avant-garde cinema than anything else being made in Japan at the time. The film was believed lost for over 40 years until Kinugasa found a surviving print in his own storehouse in 1971. It remains one of the only widely available windows into 1920s Japanese avant-garde film, a movement almost entirely wiped out by the reels lost in the following decades.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term fully expired (published 1926, well past the 95-year term).

films.title: Carnival of Souls
films.scene_label: The ghoul dance at the pavilion
films.scene_description: Under the pavilion's string lights, a ghoulish pale-faced dancer tilts her head back mid-embrace, dark hollowed eyes turned toward the camera as the other dancers move around her.
films.commentary: Carnival of Souls was made on a shoestring budget by an industrial-film director, Herk Harvey, who financed it himself and shot it in three weeks using a cast of mostly local actors. It flopped on release and was barely seen again until it turned up on late-night television in the 1970s, where its dreamlike dread found the cult audience the theatrical run never did. Directors from George Romero to David Lynch have cited it as a direct influence, and the film's copyright lapsed into the public domain almost immediately after release when the required renewal was never filed.
films.pd_basis: US copyright term expired via non-renewal (released 1962; the required renewal filing was never made).
